questions.question: Name the three non-living spheres of the Earth, give the meaning of each root word, and state two things each contains.
questions.expected_answer: Lithosphere, from lithos meaning stone: rock, mountains, ocean floor, soil. Hydrosphere, from hydor meaning water: oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, ice and water vapour in clouds. Atmosphere: the layer of gases around the Earth, mostly nitrogen (about 78 per cent) and oxygen (about 21 per cent), with a little carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.question: Define the biosphere and explain why dead organic matter is included in it. Use a pond to show how all four spheres can be found in one place.
questions.expected_answer: The biosphere is the zone where the lithosphere, hydrosphere and atmosphere overlap and life exists; it includes all living organisms and dead organic matter. Dead matter is included because decomposers such as fungi, bacteria and earthworms break it down and return nutrients to the soil for plants, so it remains part of the living system. A pond: water is the hydrosphere; mud and stones are the lithosphere; dissolved air and the air above it are the atmosphere; frogs, reeds, algae and rotting leaves are the biosphere.

questions.question: Describe one way water moves between the spheres and one way carbon moves between them. Then explain how overgrazing can affect three spheres.
questions.expected_answer: Water: the Sun evaporates water from the sea (hydrosphere) into the atmosphere; plants transpire water vapour; it condenses into clouds and falls as rain, soaking into soil (lithosphere) or being taken up by roots (biosphere). Carbon: plants take carbon dioxide from the atmosphere for photosynthesis and release oxygen; plants and animals release carbon dioxide when they respire, and decomposers release it from dead matter. Overgrazing removes plant cover (biosphere), so rain erodes the bare soil (lithosphere), which is carried by rivers and settles as silt in dams (hydrosphere), reducing their storage.
